idiom_name: Map<string, Entity[]> keyed by 'cx,cy' cell strings
implementation_notes: The classic structure is hand-written with a Map of arrays: the cell key is a string such as cx,cy and the value a plain array of entity references; Map provides sublinear lookup, accepts any key and iterates predictably (MDN Map). This is the default in browser game and simulation code, where per-frame updates are cheap and the index is small. For map or dataviz workloads over mostly static rectangles, rbush supplies a ready-made R-tree and eliminates the cell bookkeeping entirely.
pitfalls: Position modulo with a negative coordinate truncates toward zero; use Math.floor consistently for the cell mapping.
Cell arrays are never deleted unless empty cells are pruned, so memory grows with the area ever visited.
Map is per-realm: worker threads cannot share it, and a SharedArrayBuffer grid needs explicit synchronisation.

variants.name: RBush R-tree
variants.idiom_name: new RBush() with insert/remove/search over bounding boxes
variants.implementation_notes: rbush is a widely used JavaScript R-tree: items carry minX/minY/maxX/maxY, search(bbox) returns intersecting items, remove deletes them and load() bulk-builds a tree for static data (rbush README). It replaces the hand grid when objects are rectangle-shaped and updates are much rarer than searches - maps, charts and viewport culling. For per-frame movement of many small entities a grid is cheaper because every R-tree insert or remove rebalances the tree.
pitfalls: Items are removed by reference by default; a copy needs a custom equals callback or the entry stays in the tree.
Bulk load() is much faster than repeated inserts, but loading a scattered set into an existing tree degrades query performance.
The default data format expects minX/minY/maxX/maxY; other shapes need toBBox/compareMinX/compareMinY overrides.
